ch1.testimonial: I am writing to tell you how strongly I feel about SignWriting and how much it can benefit Deaf people. I was born Deaf to a Deaf family and I am a native American Sign Language (ASL) user. I have been working with SignWriting since 1982. I was the first Deaf person to write articles in ASL, in SignWriting, for the SignWriter Newspaper. Later, Valerie Sutton and I established the Deaf Action Committee for SignWriting (the DAC) in 1988. I think it is very important to spread the word about SignWriting. ASL is a language in its own right, yet until the development of SignWriting, it was a language without a written form. When I found out about SignWriting I was thrilled to think that at last we would have a way to write our language. Deaf Americans are one of the very few linguistic minorities that are unable to get books teaching English in their native language. I feel that we can use SignWriting in order to learn English. Deaf people will benefit greatly from books explaining English grammar and idioms in written ASL. We can also use it to write down and preserve our stories, poetry and plays. As you know, there are many Deaf playwrights and poets, and up until now, they have not had a way to write the ASL in their literature. No matter what the project, SignWriting encourages us to read and write and I feel that is important. All of us hope that you will enjoy learning SignWriting. Your interest and support is a great help to our Deaf community.

ch12.shoulderLineIntro: Everything in this chapter is built on the shoulder line — a horizontal bar across the shoulders. From it the body lifts, moves, tilts, bends and twists. Click any symbol below to see it in every direction.
ch12.shouldersIntro: The shoulders hold a position — one or both raised or lowered — or move up and down on the Wall Plane, or forward and back on the Floor Plane.
ch12.torsoIntro: The whole upper body stretches up or sinks down, curves and bends to the side, twists left or right, or tilts from the ribcage.
ch12.tiltsSubhead: Rocking Motion from the Hip Joint
ch12.tiltsIntro: The upper body tilts or rocks back and forth. The neck and torso do not bend — they stay straight, moving as a unit from the hip joints.

ch11.rimBack: Rim of the Back of the Head
ch11.rimTop: Rim of the Top of the Head
ch11.rimSide: Rim of the Side of the Head
ch11.headIntro: The Head is written as a circle, read from different viewpoints — front, back, side or top — shown by small marks on the rim: a nose triangle for a side view, a bar or diamond for a top view, a double arc for the back.
ch11.contactIntro: A Contact Center star marks the spot where contact is made. It sits in the middle of any viewpoint.
ch11.rimIntro: The Rim marks a place on the edge of the head. Each rim symbol rotates to eight positions around the circle, naming a spot on the face, the back, the top or the side of the head. Click a symbol to see every position.
ch11.relatingIntro: A rim symbol written beside a sign means the hand is relating to that part of the head.
ch11.movementIntro: Click a movement symbol to see it rotated into every direction. Extra arrowheads on the symbol show the movement repeating or going back and forth.
ch11.headDirectionIntro: The entire head travels in the direction of the arrows. The nose remains straight and the neck does not bend.
ch11.faceDirectionIntro: The nose moves in the direction of the arrows. The neck bends and stretches as the nose moves.
ch11.faceLinesIntro: This is not movement — it is a stable position. The horizontal bar is the shoulders; the stem marks the direction the nose and face point, relating to the shoulders. One symbol writes the nose pointing up or down; the other adds a head tilt. Click to see every position.

punctuation.english: similar to a Comma in English
similar to a Period in English
similar to a Semi-Colon in English

punctuation.term: QUESTIONING PAUSE BEFORE END OF PHRASE
punctuation.english: similar to a Question Mark in English
punctuation.detail: When a sentence or phrase ends in a question, there is a slight pause at the end. The semi-colon symbol is used to write that pause at the end, but it must be combined with signs that write the grammatically necessary Facial Expressions and Head Movements that occur in sign languages when asking questions, including Head Forward and Eyebrows Up or Down.

punctuation.english: similar to a Colon in English
punctuation.detail: This is used in the middle of a sentence, marking a new phrase that lists items 1, 2, 3 and so on.
Marks a second thought inside a sentence, starting with the curved-up symbol and ending in the curved-down parentheses.

ch14.dyn1: SignWriting, like other writing systems, has punctuation. A dark line at the end of a SignWriting sentence is the equivalent to a period in English. It marks the end of the sentence or phrase. Two lines represent a pause, or comma.
ch14.dyn2: SignWriting can add more feeling to sentences by adding Dynamics Symbols to the Punctuation.
ch14.dyn3: The Fast Symbol represents a sentence executed quickly, with speed. This is similar to an Exclamation Point in English.
ch14.dyn4: Slow, Smooth, Tense and Relaxed Dynamic Symbols can also be placed near Punctuation Symbols to give the feeling of slow, smooth, tense or relaxed sentences.
ch14.readingIntro: Punctuation in context, written in vertical SignWriting columns. The Period and Pause lines close each thought; the annotations mark the Facial Expressions, Head Movements and Dynamics that carry the meaning.
ch14.cap1: English Translation: Writing ASL from the Deaf perspective.
ch14.cap2: English Translation: Where is the house?
ch14.cap3: English Translation: Baby Bear asks “Who are you?” Goldilocks saw the bears, became frightened, shot out of the house, and ran all the way home.

ch10.intro: Facial expressions are written inside the Facial Circle. Each feature — the forehead, eyebrows, eyes, eyegaze, ears, cheeks, nose, breathing, mouth, tongue, teeth and chin — has its own group of symbols placed where it sits on the face.
ch10.neutralText: The empty circle is the face seen straight on. Every expression is built by adding symbols to it.
ch10.convention: Right and left, both at once. Paired features — eyebrows, eyes, ears, cheeks — are written for both sides, the right side alone, or the left side alone (right and left are the signer’s own). Directional features — eyegaze, tongue, chin — are rotated to point where they go. Click any symbol below to see its variants.
ch10.sideHint: Both at once, the right side alone, or the left side alone.

intros.eyebrows: Eyebrows are written above the eyes. The straight eyebrows lift up, rest neutral, or pull down; the dreamy eyebrows curve.
intros.eyegaze: Eyegaze shows where the eyes look. Wall-plane gaze moves up and down the front wall; floor-plane gaze moves forward and back.
intros.chin: The jaw moves on two planes: wall-plane chin movement points up and down, floor-plane chin movement points forward and back.

ch13.caption: Dynamics symbols mark the speed, timing and quality of movement, handshapes, faces and whole phrases.
categories: Movement Dynamics are small symbols placed near movement arrows. They indicate movement that is fast, slow, smooth, tense, relaxed, simultaneous, alternating, and uneven-alternating.
Handshape Dynamics mark classifiers. They mark a hand that is held in one place for a long time.
Facial Dynamics show tense or relaxed facial muscles. The Tense Symbol is used for lips that press together, for raised cheeks, and for squeezed eyes.
Punctuation Dynamics show the speed, timing and quality of entire phrases and sentences.
Unit Dynamics marks the influence of one symbol on a whole group of signs. The Unit-Connecting Line is used to show one facial expression influencing several signs.

movement.title: Simultaneous Line
movement.body: Both hands move at the same time.

movement.title: Alternating Lines
movement.body: The right hand moves in one direction, while the left moves simultaneously in the opposite direction.

movement.title: Un-Even Alternating — One Moves While The Other One Is Still
movement.body: The right hand moves while the left remains still. Then the left moves while the right remains still.

ch13.cl1: Classifiers are written with the handshape, plus a Classifier Marker. The Classifier Marker is a Tension Symbol. It is placed under the handshape.
ch13.cl2: In this sentence, Goldilocks sees a bowl of porridge. The bowl is established in space by a feeling of tension, a little like the feeling of placing something on a table. It anchors the visual picture of a bowl in space. The Tension Symbol marks that feeling. It is always placed under the handshapes.
ch13.cl3: Once the classifier is established, one hand continues to mark the classifier, held in the same position, while the other hand does other signs. The Tension Symbol remains under the hand that marks the classifier.
ch13.cl4: Goldilocks is discussing the porridge. She is saying that she sees the bowl, and then eats the porridge from it. But the porridge is too hot!!
ch13.facialHeading: Facial Dynamics Related To Handshape Dynamics
ch13.fac1: Facial expressions are essential to writing Sign Language stories and literature. They mark grammar and emphasis. The Tense Lips symbol shows the dynamics of the lips tensing as the hand is established in space by a classifier. Tension on the lips and near the hands are oftentimes written together.
ch13.fac2: Below: The Classifier for "bed" in American Sign Language is written with a Tension Symbol under the handshape to mark the classifier. At the same time, the lips also tense, giving the feeling of "anchoring the classifier" in space.
bedPlacements: This bed is placed to the left side. It is established in the left space, to the left of the facial expression. The lips tense as the classifier is placed in space.
This bed is placed in the center. It is established in the center space, directly under the facial expression. The lips tense as the classifier is placed in space.
This bed is placed to the right side. It is established in the right space, to the right of the facial expression. The lips tense as the classifier is placed in space.

ch13.u1: Influence is written with a Unit-Connecting Line.
ch13.u2: The Unit-Connecting Line is useful for Sign Language researchers. It is used to show the influence of one facial expression on a group of signs.
ch13.u3: When one symbol influences a group of symbols or signs, the symbol that is influencing the group is written first. Then a line is written, like a bracket, connecting the symbol with the group it influences.
ch13.u4: When SignWriting is written vertically, the Unit-Connecting Line is written to the side of the vertical column, as shown here. The Unit Line is grey or lighter than the signs.
ch13.u5: In Spain, the Unit-Connecting Line is used for horizontal SignWriting literature. When writing horizontally, the Unit-Connecting Line is written under or over the writing.
ch13.u6: In Sutton DanceWriting, the Unit-Connecting Line is used often to show the influence of one movement symbol on a group of other symbols. In SignWriting, it is rarely used for everyday use.

ch9.armIntro: Arm circles parallel to the Wall Plane are double-stemmed circles. Arrows mark exactly where the circular movement starts. When reading Circle Symbols, place your hand where the arrows are located on the circle, and then move in the direction of the arrows.
ch9.wristIntro: Wrist circles are written with solid lines. Arrows are placed outside the circle. When reading Wrist Circle Symbols, place your hand at the arrow, and then move in that direction.

ch7.wallIntro: Up-Down movement is parallel with the front wall. It is written with double-stemmed arrows:
ch7.upDownArrowsIntro: The curves are parallel with the wall.
ch7.floorIntro: Forward-Back movement is parallel with the floor. It is written with single-stemmed arrows. The thinner section of the arrow means far from the body; the thick, dark section means close to the body — like looking down a road, close is wider and darker.

ch8.intro: There are two types of Axial Movement:
ch8.rot1: SignWriting includes symbols which show rotation movements made with your forearm. The forearm does not travel. It stays in one place and rotates.
ch8.rot2: Rotation Symbols place a curved arrow on an "axis". The "axis-line" represents the forearm. The rotation revolves around this axis.
ch8.foreUpIntro: A double-lined axis-line represents an axis that is parallel with the wall. The forearm is up and the rotation revolves around this up-down axis:

rose1.bottom: Thumb leads — back toward the chest, then side.
rose1.right: Baby finger leads — side, forward, then side again.
rose1.left: Thumb leads — side, back, then side again.

ch8.rose1Note: Note: The top and bottom movements are technically the same. The difference is the feeling of the baby finger or the feeling of the thumb leading the rotation — some signs push and some signs pull.
ch8.foreForwardIntro: A single-lined "axis-line" represents an axis parallel with the floor. When the forearm is pointing forward, parallel with the floor, the "axis-line" is a single line pointing forward:

rose2.right: Baby finger leads — side, down, then side again.
rose2.left: Thumb leads — side, up, then side again.

ch8.exUpHeading: Rotation, Forearm Up — Parallel with Front Wall
ch8.exForwardHeading: Rotation, Forearm Forward — Parallel with Floor
ch8.foreSideIntro: When the forearm is parallel with the floor, but pointing side, the "axis-line" is a single horizontal line pointing side.
ch8.exSideHeading: Rotation, Forearm Side — Parallel with Floor
ch8.travelIntro: A few movement symbols combine "traveling" movement with an added rotation. The forearm rotates as the arm moves in a specific direction. The rotation symbol is placed on the stem line of the arrow.
ch8.shakeIntro: Shaking Rotation does not define how many rotations you make. Instead, it is a fast, shaking motion. It can be written with or without an arrowhead. The dark and light arrowheads are needed at times, to show which arm is doing the shaking.
ch8.shakeWallLabel: Shaking Movement, Forearm Up or Down — Parallel with the Wall Plane
ch8.shakeFloorLabel: Shaking Movement, Forearm Forward — Parallel with the Floor Plane
ch8.wristIntro: The wrist remains stable while the hand moves in different directions. This flexing motion is written with a horizontal line cutting the wrist. The horizontal line represents the axis of motion. Small arrows point in the direction of the flexing motion. The arrows represent the direction of the hand as it moves.
ch8.flag:
ASL Sign For "Flag"
Wrist Flexing Forward and Back Towards the Chest

ch6.wallIntro: The Wall Plane is parallel with the front wall.
ch6.floorIntro: The Floor Plane is parallel with the floor.
ch6.gen1: When a right movement arrow writes ON TOP OF a left movement arrow, the two movement paths overlap each other. The two arrows blend together. The dark arrowhead and the light arrowhead become one arrowhead, called the General Arrowhead.
ch6.gen2: Often the hands are contacting when moving in overlapping paths, but it is NOT ONLY for contacting hands. For example, two hands can be parallel, side by side, without contact, and then both move to the same side, so that the right arrow writes on top of the left arrow. This creates a General Arrowhead.
ch6.upDownIntro: Up-Down Movement is parallel with the Front Wall or your chest. It is written with double-stemmed arrows. Movement with the right hand uses a dark arrowhead; movement with the left hand uses a light arrowhead. Remember! SignWriting is written from the expressive point of view, so it is most correct looking at this from the back.
ch6.fwBackIntro: Forward-Back Movement is parallel with the Floor or a table top. It is written with single-stemmed arrows. Movement with the right hand uses a dark arrowhead; movement with the left hand uses a light arrowhead.
ch6.sideIntro: Movement to the side can be viewed from either the Front View or the Top View. It can be written with either double-stemmed or single-stemmed arrows.
ch6.upOrDownIntro: A double-stemmed arrow means that the movement is straight up or down, parallel with the front wall. The movement is flat with the front of your body.
ch6.fwOrBackIntro: A single-stemmed arrow means that the movement is forward or back, parallel with the floor. You are looking down, on top of the movement.
ch6.upDownStraightIntro: Up-Down movement is parallel with the Front Wall. It is written with double-stemmed arrows.
ch6.fwBackStraightIntro: Forward-Back movement is parallel with the floor. It is written with single-stemmed arrows.
ch6.fwBackArrowsIntro: Straight movement parallel with the floor.
ch6.recap1: Let's review what we have already learned.
ch6.recap2: Writing movement is based on imaginary planes that cut space. The Plane that is parallel with the front wall, is called the Wall Plane. Up-Down Movement is parallel with the Wall Plane. It is written with double-stemmed arrows.
ch6.recap3: The Plane that is parallel with the floor, is called the Floor Plane. Forward-Back Movement is parallel with the Floor Plane. It is written with single-stemmed arrows.
ch6.recap4: Imagine a rocketship that travels straight up. Up Movement is written with double-stemmed arrows.
ch6.recap5: Imagine driving a car. Think of the line in the center of the road. Forward Movement is written with single-stemmed arrows.
ch6.diag1: Space is also divided by diagonal planes. The Up-Diagonal Plane starts low at your feet and extends up towards the front wall. It is both forward and up.
ch6.diag2: A horizontal bar means away from your chest. A dot means towards your chest.
ch6.upFwDiagIntro: Imagine an airplane taking off, traveling toward the horizon. Up-Forward-Diagonal-Movement is written with a double-stemmed arrow. A horizontal line, representing the horizon, crosses the stemline.
ch6.downBackDiagIntro: Imagine an airplane coming in for a landing, traveling towards you. Down-Back-Diagonal Movement is written with double-stemmed arrows. A dark dot is written on the stem of the arrow. The dot represents the nose of the plane as it is coming towards you.

ch2.intro: SignWriting can be written from either the Receptive or the Expressive viewpoints. This book teaches reading and writing signs from the Expressive Viewpoint. The Expressive Viewpoint is now the standard in SignWriting publications. The Receptive Viewpoint is used occasionally when transcribing signs from videotape, or when recording foreign signs in shorthand. For more information on using the Receptive Viewpoint, refer to <ch15>Chapter 15</ch15>.
ch2.expressiveIntro: When you are signing to someone else, you see signs from your own point of view. This is called the Expressive Viewpoint.
ch2.receptiveIntro: When someone is facing you, signing to you, you view the signs as an observer. The signer's right side is your left side. This is called the Receptive Viewpoint.
ch2.expressiveMainIntro: Read and write signs as if you are looking at your own hands, from your own perspective.
ch2.palmIntro: When you see the palm of your hand, while you are signing, the symbol for the hand will be white, or hollow. The palm of the hand is always written with a white, hollow symbol.
ch2.side1: When you see the side of your hand while you are signing, the symbol for the hand will be half black and half white.
ch2.side2: The white part of the symbol shows where the palm of the hand faces. The dark part represents the back of the hand.
ch2.back1: When you see the back of your hand while you are signing, the symbol will be black, or filled-in.
ch2.back2: The back of the hand is always written with a black, filled-in symbol.
ch2.sidesHeadIntro: The head is written with a circle, viewed from the back. The symbol for the hand is placed on the side of the head it is near. In ASL, this sign means "know". An asterisk means touch.
ch2.sidesFaceIntro: Pretend you can see through the back of the head. You are reading and writing how your face feels when you sign. In ASL, this sign also means "know". Two asterisks mean touching two times.

ch15.pc1: When starting to write a sign, ask yourself: "Is there a Position of Contact in this sign?". Are the hands contacting each other? Are the hands contacting the Face or Body? Write that Position of Contact first, which becomes the "Center of the Sign".
ch15.pc2: When writing the Position of Contact, try to place the two contacting symbols as close to each other as possible. Try to make it look like it does in real life. There should be very little space between the two contacting symbols.
ch15.pc3: SignSpellings revolve around the Position of Contact like a small universe. The Position of Contact is the Center of the Sign, and the Movement and Contact Symbols relate to that center.
ch15.correctCaption: Correct — Position of Contact is the Center of the Sign.
ch15.incorrectCaption: Incorrect — Sign is too spread out and the focus is missing.
ch15.pc4: The Position of Contact is important because it holds the meaning in a sign. The eye focuses on the Position of Contact when reading. The Position of Contact is like a unit.
ch15.pc5: Writing the Position of Contact also creates smaller signs in width and height, which makes writing in vertical columns more centered and compact, making the columns themselves less wide.
ch15.pc6: Writing the Position of Contact gives a visual picture of the sign. Since you can see the two hands are touching by their close placement, the single Touch Contact Star is rarely necessary. It is not wrong to write the single Touch Contact Star, but it is not necessary either. This simplifies the writing of signs.
ch15.pc7: Double Touch Contact Stars are written no matter what, because Double Touch, or Touch-Touch, is a movement, not a position. It is only single Touch Contact Stars that can be eliminated.
ch15.pc8: The two contacting symbols, such as the Hands and Face, are written close to each other. Then Movement Symbols are placed nearby.
ch15.pc9: Sometimes the entire sign is nothing but the Position of Contact, with no other symbols needed.
ch15.center1: Every sign has a Center, like a little universe (the Sun is the center and the planets rotate around it). The Center of the Sign gives the sign focus for the reader. It is an Anchor, that grabs your attention.
ch15.center2: The Position of Contact is usually the Center of the Sign:
ch15.meetCaption: MEET (ASL) — Position of Contact is the Center of this Sign.
ch15.seeCaption: SEE (ASL) — Position of Contact is the Center of this Sign.
ch15.noContactIntro: If there is <term>no</term> contact, then the Beginning Position is the Center:
ch15.curtainsCaption: CURTAINS (ASL) — Beginning Handshapes are the Center of this Sign.
ch15.youCaption: YOU (ASL) — Beginning Handshape is the Center of this Sign.
ch15.arrow1: The Position of Contact is written first. It is the Center of the sign.
ch15.arrow2: There are 8 possible placements of Movement Symbols around the Center. Each arrow <term>pulls</term> or <term>drags</term> the hands in its direction, and keeps the same spatial relationship to the Center as it has on the Wheel.
ch15.wallGuide1: Straight movement parallel with the front wall is written with double-stemmed arrows.
ch15.wallGuide2: Hover each arrow on the wheel to see the sign it writes. The arrow stays where it sits on the wheel: the up arrow is placed above the Center, the down arrow below, the side arrows to the left or right, and the diagonals above- or below-and-to-the-side.
ch15.floorGuide1: Straight movement parallel with the floor is written with single-stemmed arrows.
ch15.floorGuide2: Hover each arrow to see the sign it writes. The forward arrow is placed above the Center (the movement travels away from your chest), the back arrow below (toward your chest), and the diagonals above- or below-and-to-the-side.
ch15.curveGuide1: If the movement is <term>curved</term>, choose the curve arrow you need. Like the straight arrows, each curve keeps the same spatial relationship to the Center as it has on the Wheel.
ch15.curveGuide2: Hover each arrow to see the sign it writes — a curve above the Center curves over the top, a curve below curves under, and so on around the wheel.
ch15.rotationIntro: If the movement is a <term>rotation arrow</term>, choose the <term>rotation arrow</term> needed. Keep the <term>rotation arrow</term> in the same spatial-relationship to the <term>center</term> as it was when all the other arrows were in the Wheel.
ch15.rotationPlacement: If the curve of the Rotation Arrow is curved down, it is usually placed under the hands. If the curve of the Rotation Arrow is curved up, then it is usually placed above the hands.
ch15.rotationPlacementAlt: Rotation arrows placed above or below the hands depending on their curve
ch15.exception: EXCEPTION: Occasionally arrows can collide with other symbols, such as the Facial Circle or the Shoulder Line. When this happens there is no choice but to place the Movement Arrow a little to the side to avoid the collision. This happens mostly when contacting the Face.
